pull.title: KAFKA-19023: Implement snapshottable timers in the coordinator runtime
pull.body:
This PoC makes `CoordinatorTimerImpl` snapshottable, aligning timer
state restoration with the Coordinator’s snapshot and rollback
lifecycle.

The main changes are:

1. `CoordinatorTimerImpl` stores a `TimerState` for each timer in a
`TimelineHashMap`, using the same `SnapshotRegistry` as the Coordinator.
2. `TimerState` contains the information needed to recreate a
`TimerTask`: its deadline, operation, and retry configuration. Scheduled
`TimerTask` instances are managed separately.
3. When a record append succeeds, the existing
`updateLastWrittenOffset(offset)` flow creates a snapshot at that
offset, including the timer state. Scheduled tasks continue running
unchanged.
4. If the append fails, `revertLastWrittenOffset()` restores the timer
state to the rollback target snapshot.
5. After restoring the state, `timer.onRollback()` cancels all currently
tracked tasks and schedules new tasks based on the restored `TimerState
entries`. Each task uses the time remaining until its original deadline,
or a delay of zero if the deadline has already passed

Reviewers: Sean Quah <squah@confluent.io>, David Jacot
 <dajac@apache.org>

review_comments.body:
@chickenchickenlove Thanks for the patch! Does it mean that we must cancel and re-schedule all the timers on rollbacks? This seems pretty expensive, isn't it?

I'd like to suggest an alternative design. One approach would be to only keep the timers made by the operations of the current batch as pending until the batch is successfully written. When it is, the pending timers are moved to the "committed" space. If the write fails, they are dropped. We don't really need to full-fleshed rollback to any previous committed offset in the timer case.

It basically means that a timer is not really overridden until committed. In this case, we must define what to do if the previous one fires before the new one is committed. This may also be true in your design.

I have not tested it. It is just an idea. Thoughts?

@chickenchickenlove @dajac I tried the batch-based approach for the coordinator executor in https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/23923. The names of the commit/revert methods are tbd we should align on them. The requirements for the executor look a lot more relaxed than timers - we only need to cancel tasks on a rollback and can rely on the next heartbeat to re-schedule tasks.

@dajac 
Agree. This implementation is expensive and not scalable because of time complexity.  (@squah-confluent also, thanks for taking time to look into this!)
I've given some thought to the approach based on your suggestions. What do you think of this implementation? 

1. Timer `A` is scheduled with a deadline of 20. There is no pending timer.
2. The coordinator schedules a replacement, Timer `B`, with the same key and a deadline of 40. `A` remains scheduled, while `B` is kept pending.
3. Depending on the write result:
   - Success: The coordinator runtime calls `commit()`, cancels `A`, and schedules `B` using the remaining time until its deadline. The pending entry is cleared.
   - Failure: The coordinator runtime calls `revert()` and discards `B`. `A` remains scheduled.

There are also two cases we need to handle these
1. Operations that produce no records. If `commit()` is only called after a successful log write, their pending timer changes may never be applied. We therefore need a way to finalize these changes without a new write, while respecting any pending batch they depend on.
2. A expires while `B` is pending. We could retain `A`’s timeout operation without executing it. On `commit()`, we discard that operation and schedule `B`. On `revert()`, we discard `B` and enqueue `A`’s timeout operation for execution after the coordinator state has been rolled back.

What do you think? 
@dajac @squah-confluent When you get a chance, please take a look!! 🙇‍♂️

> 1. Operations that produce no records.

Not sure if this is 100% a match for the case you have in mind: We can "commit" instantly in `append()` when there are no records to write and there is no pending batch. (I'm still stuck on the names.)

https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/23923/changes#diff-37d422ba9671aaf4524a78e25a9c50830ca0aaf64e1979772c70e4e1198c919bR925

Agreed! I also like the method names you suggested.
I'm going to work on implementing the 2 phase approach on the `CoordinatorTimerImpl` side. 
This PR still uses TimelineHashMap for the snapshottable implementation. 😅

@dajac @squah-confluent 

I tried implementing an approach where timer changes remain pending until the batch is successfully appended to the local log. On success, the changes are applied; on failure, they are discarded.

This seems suitable for issues such as KAFKA-21279, where timer changes need to be reverted when a write fails. However, applying the same policy to all existing `schedule()` and `cancel()` calls revealed that these changes have different semantics:

1. Changes that depend on speculative coordinator state should be discarded if the corresponding write fails.
2. Timers scheduled by failure callbacks to restore the previous state must survive that recovery.
3. Changes such as extending a session timeout upon receiving a heartbeat require a separate policy decision: should they also be reverted when an unrelated write fails?

The current `schedule()` and `cancel()` APIs do not express these dependencies. Having the Runtime or TimerImpl infer them from the execution path makes the implementation more complex and risks unintentionally changing existing behavior.

What do you think about preserving the existing APIs’ immediate scheduling and cancellation behavior, while allowing callers to explicitly choose when timer changes should depend on the write outcome?

For example, `CoordinatorRuntime` could own both the existing `CoordinatorTimerImpl` and a separate `RevertableCoordinatorTimerImpl`, and expose both to the coordinator. Callers would use the existing timer for changes that should take effect immediately, and explicitly use the revertable timer for changes that should be applied or discarded based on the write outcome.

If both implementations can operate on timers with the same key, we would also need to define how replacement and cancellation interact across them, including the order in which changes are applied.

What do you think?

> 2. Timers scheduled by failure callbacks to restore the previous state must survive that recovery.

I'm expecting these to be a manual implementation of rolling back timer state. Hopefully they should all disappear at the end of this PR?

> 3. Changes such as extending a session timeout upon receiving a heartbeat require a separate policy decision: should they also be reverted when an unrelated write fails?

For simplicity I think unextending the session timeout is best. A consumer would have to miss more than one heartbeat to be evicted from a group. We could consider write failures to be rare enough that it's not worth the extra design effort. @dajac any thoughts?

issue_comments.body:
Hi, @squah-confluent !
This is a draft PoC PR for the snapshottable timer.
It is still at an early stage(not cover all details), but I think the basic implementation is mostly in place.
Could we discuss the implementation here? 

If this approach sounds good to you, I'll proceed with the implementation details.
Thanks! I'll take a look when I can!

I have not fully reviewed yet. Can we make sure we think about the case where a timer fires, tries to write records but persistently fails?

eg. the last consumer protocol member expiring from a mixed group, whose departure triggers a downgrade to a classic group and a write of a large `GroupMetadata` record. If the write is oversized and always fails, we can get stuck in a loop if we roll back the timer and re-run it.
